newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UNICEF debunks that child labor only in poor nations.
newsitem.headline: UNICEF debunks that child labor only in poor nations.

text.p: Children are bitten by snakes on rubber plantations in Malaysia, inhale pesticides picking coffee in Tanzania and are hurt on construction sites in Portugal, the U.N. Children's Fund said Wednesday.
In the United States, they can found working on large farms and in sweatshops of the garment industry, UNICEF said in a report on child labour around the world.
"Hazardous child labour must be left behind, consigned to history as completely as those other forms of slavery that it so closely resembles," said UNICEF director Carol Bellamy.

Calling for global action, UNICEF said countries should provide schooling for all children, enforce international the ties they signed and immediately end "intolerable forms of child labour such as prostitution or bonded labour."

UNICEF's report, which follows up one on the same subject several months ago by the International Labour Organisation, contended that more than 250 million children between 5-14 years were working in conditions detrimental to their health.

The report also sought to debunk myths that child labour was found only in poor nations, that it was inevitable in families of extreme poverty and that most children were employed in export industries that could be reformed through sanctions and boycotts.

Mexican-American children work on farms in New York state, including fields wet with pesticides, while children are employed by leather industries in the Naples region of Italy. And in Britain, 15 to 26 percent of the 11-year-olds and 36 to 66 percent of the 15-year-olds are working, the report said.
Nevertheless, most child labourers live in the developing world, half of them in Asia, where bonded labour is common.

Children as young as eight are pledged by their parents to factory owners or agents in exchange for very small loans. In India this type of transaction is widespread in industries such as those making carpets and matches, UNICEF said.
In Africa one child in three works and in Latin America one in five works. A survey of domestic servants in Uruguay found that 34 percent had begun working before they were 14.
Another myth, UNICEF said, is that child labour will never be eliminated until poverty disappears, thereby saying "we must tolerate the intolerable until world poverty is ended."
But the report contended that children were employed because an employer or parent benefitted from cheap labour, depriving adults of jobs.

"Poverty drives children into hazardous labour. Yet if employers were not prepared to exploit children, there would be no child labour. In other words children are employed because they are easier to exploit," UNICEF said.

And contrary to a common belief, less than five percent of children are employed in export industries. Instead they are found selling on the streets, working in agriculture and prostitution, or hidden away in homes far from the reach of official labour inspectors, the report said.

While international boycotts and sanctions against firms employing children are valuable, UNICEF warned that such actions need to include alternatives for children. Otherwise they are driven into other exploitative work.
The report also criticised the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund for its programmes that forced governments to reduce social and educational spending.
It renewed an appeal to governments to allocate 20 percent of budgets to education and basic social services and for wealthy countries to earmark such sums in aid programmes.

"It would cost an estimated $6 billion a year, on top of what is already spent, to put every child in school by the year 2000," the report said. "Yet it is less than one percent of what the world spends every year on weapons."
